title: 22. Interview: Serverless
summary: Interview Q&A for Serverless — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Serverless interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a cold start and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** A cold start is the latency penalty paid when a serverless platform must provision a new execution environment for a function that has no warm instance available. It consists of micro-VM boot (AWS Firecracker, ~125ms), runtime initialization (loading Node, Python, or JVM), and your function's init code (SDK clients, heavy imports, config fetches). Total cold-start latency ranges from ~50ms for a minimal Node function to several seconds for a JVM with Spring. Warm invocations, by contrast, add only 1–5ms of platform overhead because the runtime and your init code are already loaded. Mitigations include: keeping the function's deployment package small (avoid bundling huge dependencies); moving heavy SDK initialization to module scope so it runs once per environment; choosing lighter runtimes (Node and Python over Java); using provisioned concurrency to keep N environments always warm; invoking the function on a cron every few minutes to keep it warm (a hack that works but costs money); and fronting with a CDN or API Gateway cache for the static portions of responses. The trade-off is that provisioned concurrency and keep-warm crons partially erode the cost benefit of scale-to-zero.
**Visual:**
```
cold:  [boot microVM 125ms] + [runtime init 50ms] + [user init 100ms] = 275ms+
warm:  [dispatch 3ms] + [handler runtime]                            = ~10ms
mitigate: small pkg, lazy imports, provisioned concurrency, lighter runtime
```

### Q2. How is serverless billed, and when does it become more expensive than containers?
**Answer:** AWS Lambda bills per request (around $0.20 per million requests) plus per GB-second (memory × duration in 1-ms increments at $0.0000166667 per GB-second). A 256MB function running 200ms costs roughly 0.85 microdollars per invocation. At low volume this is dramatically cheaper than always-on containers — 100 requests a day on Lambda is essentially free, while a t3.micro container costs $8/month regardless. The crossover point comes when sustained throughput is high enough that per-request billing exceeds the cost of running an equivalent container continuously. A back-of-envelope: a 256MB container on Fargate costs about $17/month (compute + memory); the same throughput served by Lambda at 100 RPS sustained (260M requests/month) at 200ms each would cost roughly $200/month. So for workloads above a few million sustained requests per month, containers or managed Kubernetes become cheaper. The mature pattern is serverless-first for the long tail of low-volume endpoints, migrating hot paths to containers once cost signals justify it.
**Visual:**
```
Lambda cost = (reqs * $0.20/1M) + (memory_GB * duration_s * reqs * $1.67e-5)
crossover ~5-10M sustained reqs/month at 200ms, 256MB -> containers cheaper
```

### Q3. What is the difference between FaaS and other serverless managed services?
**Answer:** FaaS (Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) is serverless compute where you provide code and the platform runs it per event. Other serverless managed services provide entire capabilities without you writing or running compute at all. DynamoDB is serverless storage with autoscaling throughput — no EC2, no Cassandra cluster to operate. S3 is serverless object storage. API Gateway is serverless HTTP routing. SQS, SNS, and EventBridge are serverless messaging. Cognito is serverless identity. Aurora Serverless v2 is serverless relational database. Step Functions is serverless workflow orchestration. The shared properties are: no infrastructure to manage, automatic scaling, pay-per-use billing, and high availability built in. The distinction matters because a typical serverless application is mostly composed of managed services with FaaS used only for the custom logic that connects them — the "Lambda" portion is often 10% of the architecture, with DynamoDB, S3, and API Gateway carrying the bulk.
**Visual:**
```
FaaS:           you write code  -> Lambda runs it per event
managed svc:    you configure   -> DynamoDB/S3/SQS/API Gateway run themselves
serverless app: API GW -> Lambda -> DynamoDB  (Lambda is small slice of arch)
```

### Q4. Why are serverless functions stateless, and where do you put state?
**Answer:** Serverless functions are stateless because the platform can spin up or tear down execution environments at any time, and a single warm environment may serve many concurrent invocations or none for hours. Any state held in process memory is unreliable — it may disappear at any moment, it is not shared between environments, and it cannot be relied on for the next invocation. This forces a functional programming style: pure functions that take an event, do work, return a result, and persist any durable state to an external service. State goes in DynamoDB (key-value), S3 (objects/blobs), Aurora Serverless (relational), ElastiCache or Redis (low-latency cache), or SQS (work queues). For session state, use DynamoDB with a session ID. For files, use S3 and pass the key. For workflow state, use Step Functions which manages state externally. The trade-off is that every state operation is a network call, adding latency and cost; the benefit is horizontal scale without coordination and resilience to environment failure.
**Visual:**
```
Lambda (stateless)  --read/write-->  DynamoDB (durable state)
                    --persist-->     S3 (blobs)
                    --cache-->       ElastiCache (low latency)
                    --queue-->       SQS (work backlog)
                    --orchestrate--> Step Functions (workflow state)
```

### Q5. What are the concurrency limits in serverless, and how do you handle bursts?
**Answer:** AWS Lambda has an account-wide concurrency limit (default 1000, raisable by support ticket) that caps the number of simultaneous executions across all functions in a region. Each function can also have a reserved concurrency (a guaranteed slice) and a provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed capacity). When invocations exceed the limit, the platform throttles with a 429 (TooManyRequests) and retries depend on the source — synchronous API Gateway calls fail in the response, while async EventBridge invocations are retried with exponential backoff. Bursts are handled by: requesting a quota increase if your workload legitimately needs more; using reserved concurrency to protect critical functions from being starved by a noisy neighbor in your own account; using SQS as a buffer so a downstream function processes at its own pace; using Step Functions for long-running orchestrations that should not count against concurrency; and sharding work across regions for the truly extreme case. Lambda also has a rapid burst allowance (initial 3000 concurrent invocations per second) before throttling kicks in.
**Visual:**
```
account concurrency: 1000 (default, raisable)
function reserved:    e.g. 200 reserved for critical-svc
burst allowance:      3000 concurrent/sec initial
overflow:             429 throttle -> retry w/ backoff, or queue in SQS
```

### Q6. How does serverless handle long-running workloads?
**Answer:** FaaS platforms cap execution time: AWS Lambda at 15 minutes, Google Cloud Functions Gen 2 at 60 minutes, Azure Functions on the consumption plan at 10 minutes (extended on premium). Workloads that exceed this — video transcoding, large batch jobs, ML training, complex aggregations — must be split or moved. The standard pattern is to use Step Functions or EventBridge to orchestrate a workflow of small Lambda functions, each doing a unit of work and chaining to the next via a queue or state machine. For embarrassingly parallel work like image processing, fan out via SNS to many Lambda invocations, each handling one item. For jobs that exceed 15 minutes, run them on Fargate, ECS, EKS, or Batch, triggered by a Lambda. For ML training, use SageMaker training jobs. For real-time streams, use Kinesis Data Analytics or Lambda with the streaming invoke mode (newer feature for long-lived stream processing). The trade-off is that splitting work introduces orchestration complexity and per-step latency.
**Visual:**
```
long job (45 min)  -- not OK in Lambda (15 min cap)
   -> split into 3 chunks of 15 min via Step Functions
   -> or move to Fargate / Batch, triggered by Lambda
   -> or fan out parallel items via SNS -> N Lambdas
```

### Q7. What is the trade-off between serverless and containers for a new microservice?
**Answer:** Serverless wins on operational simplicity (no servers, autoscaling built in, no patching), on cost at low volume (pay per request, zero when idle), and on velocity (deploy in minutes). It loses on per-request cost at high volume, on cold-start latency, on bounded execution (15-minute cap), on language and library constraints, on local development friction (emulating the cloud locally is hard), on observability (distributed across many services), and on vendor lock-in (each provider's event model differs). Containers win on per-request cost at high volume, on latency consistency (no cold starts), on flexibility (any language, any library, any binary), on local dev parity with production, and on portability across clouds via Kubernetes. They lose on operational complexity (cluster management, autoscaling tuning, security patching) and on idle cost (you pay for nodes whether or not they are busy). The decision rule: serverless-first for event-driven, low-volume, or spiky workloads; containers for steady high-throughput, latency-sensitive, or long-running workloads; managed databases for state in both.
**Visual:**
```
serverless:  + ops simple, + low-volume cost, + velocity
             - cold start, - 15min cap, - lock-in, - observability gap
containers:  + high-volume cost, + latency, + flexibility, + portability
             - ops complex, - idle cost, - scaling tuning
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You have a Lambda that processes S3 uploads and suddenly throughput drops. How do you debug?
**Answer:** S3 notifications to Lambda are async invocations; when Lambda throttles, S3 retries, but if retries exhaust the event is sent to a Dead Letter Queue. First, check CloudWatch Metrics for the function: `Invocations`, `Errors`, `Throttles`, `Duration`, `ConcurrentExecutions`. A spike in `Throttles` indicates the account or function concurrency limit was hit. If `Errors` is spiking, check CloudWatch Logs for the function — common causes are bad input shape (S3 event version differences), missing IAM permissions on the source bucket or downstream resources, or downstream service timeouts. If `Duration` is at the 15-minute cap, your function is timing out — likely because a downstream (DynamoDB, an external API) is slow, or because the file is too large to process in one invocation. Look at `IteratorAge` if it is a stream-based trigger; high iterator age means the function cannot keep up. Fixes: increase memory (which also scales CPU), shard the workload into smaller chunks via SNS fan-out, request a concurrency quota increase, or move heavy processing to Fargate triggered by the Lambda.
**Visual:**
```
CloudWatch:  Invocations? Errors? Throttles? Duration? ConcurrentExec?
            -> Throttles high: raise concurrency, add reserved
            -> Errors high:    check logs, IAM, input shape
            -> Duration cap:   raise memory, shard via SNS, or move to Fargate
            -> IteratorAge:    function can't keep up; scale out
```

### Q2. A user-facing API backed by Lambda has p99 latency of 800ms; users complain. What do you do?
**Answer:** First, instrument the function to break down where the 800ms goes — platform overhead (cold start), init code, downstream DB calls, downstream API calls, computation. CloudWatch Logs with `console.time` markers or AWS X-Ray traces will reveal the breakdown. If cold starts are a major contributor (check the `InitDuration` field in logs), enable provisioned concurrency for the function or apply `snapstart` (for Java/Python). If downstream DynamoDB calls are slow, check for hot partitions, consider switching from query to a cache (DynamoDB Accelerator, DAX), and ensure you are using connection reuse (the AWS SDK reuses HTTPS connections only if you create the client outside the handler). If an external API is slow, add a timeout and a circuit breaker, and consider async decoupling via SQS so the user gets a fast ack. If computation is heavy, raise memory (Lambda scales CPU linearly with memory, so 1GB runs ~4x faster than 256MB for CPU-bound work and the cost may even drop). Also check API Gateway: enable caching for GETs, use the right endpoint type (regional vs edge).
**Visual:**
```
p99 800ms breakdown:
  cold start    -> provisioned concurrency, snapstart
  DB latency    -> DAX cache, hot partition fix, connection reuse
  external API  -> timeout + circuit breaker, async via SQS
  compute heavy -> raise memory (CPU scales with memory)
  API Gateway   -> enable caching, regional endpoint
```

### Q3. You are designing a video upload pipeline. Where does serverless fit?
**Answer:** A video pipeline has distinct stages with different compute characteristics, and serverless fits some but not all. Upload: clients upload to S3 via a presigned URL issued by a Lambda (or directly via API Gateway + Lambda). Trigger: S3 event notifies a Lambda when the upload completes — this Lambda kicks off encoding. Encoding itself is CPU- and GPU-heavy and runs for minutes to hours — this is NOT a good fit for Lambda; instead, the trigger Lambda submits a job to AWS Elemental MediaConvert, AWS Batch, or Fargate. Progress tracking: encoding jobs emit events to EventBridge, which a Lambda consumes to update DynamoDB with progress. Thumbnail generation: small enough to fit in Lambda. Notification: when complete, a Lambda publishes to SNS, which fans out to push notifications and CDNs. Netflix's pipeline follows this exact pattern — Lambda for trigger and orchestration, dedicated encoders on EC2 for the heavy lifting. The lesson: serverless shines for orchestration and glue; heavy compute moves to specialized services.
**Visual:**
```
client -> presigned URL (Lambda) -> S3 upload
   S3 event -> Lambda (trigger) -> MediaConvert / Fargate (encode, heavy)
   encode events -> EventBridge -> Lambda (progress) -> DynamoDB
   complete -> Lambda -> SNS -> push + CDN
```

### Q4. Your team wants to migrate a Java monolith to Lambda. What do you tell them?
**Answer:** Java is the worst-fit mainstream language for Lambda because of cold start. The JVM init time plus a Spring or Micronaut context can easily reach 5–10 seconds, which is unusable for synchronous APIs. Before recommending the migration, push back on whether Lambda is the right target — a Java monolith on Fargate or EKS may be a better fit. If Lambda is genuinely the goal, the path is: first, decompose the monolith into small functions, each with a minimal init (use the AWS SDK v2 with lazy clients, avoid Spring, prefer Micronaut or Quarkus which compile to native images). Second, enable Lambda SnapStart (supported for Java 11+) which restores from a snapshot instead of running init — this cuts cold start from seconds to ~200ms. Third, use provisioned concurrency for user-facing functions where latency matters. Fourth, restructure as event-driven so most invocations are async and cold-start latency is less visible. Fifth, set realistic expectations: a Java Lambda will never match a Node Lambda on cold start, but with SnapStart and provisioned concurrency it can be acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
Java monolith -> decompose -> small Java Lambdas with minimal init
             -> enable SnapStart (snapshot restore, ~200ms cold)
             -> provisioned concurrency for user-facing
             -> restructure to event-driven (async, cold start less visible)
             -> consider Fargate/EKS instead if latency is critical
```

### Q5. You need to run a Lambda that reads from Kinesis at high throughput. How do you design it?
**Answer:** Kinesis-to-Lambda uses a poller that the platform operates; it batches records from the stream and invokes your function with up to 10,000 records or 10 MB per invocation. The key metric is `IteratorAge` — the age of the oldest record in the stream — which tells you whether you are keeping up. If iterator age is climbing, you are not consuming fast enough. Levers: increase the number of shards (each shard is processed in parallel by a separate Lambda invocation up to the concurrency limit); increase batch size to process more records per invocation; tune parallelization factor (Lambda can process up to 10 batches per shard concurrently); use `MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds` to balance latency vs throughput; raise the function's memory (and thus CPU) so it processes the batch faster; offload heavy work to a downstream queue (SQS) and let Lambda fan out. If a single batch takes too long, split it: process each record by pushing to SQS for finer-grained parallelism. Watch for poison-pill records — configure `BisectBatchOnFunctionError` so a failing batch is split in half to isolate the bad record, and route failures to a DLQ.
**Visual:**
```
Kinesis shard 1 -> batch -> Lambda inv A
Kinesis shard 2 -> batch -> Lambda inv B    (parallel across shards)
   within shard: parallelization factor up to 10x
   iterator age climbing? -> more shards, larger batch, raise memory
   poison pill? -> BisectBatchOnFunctionError -> isolate -> DLQ
```

### Q6. You are building a webhook receiver that gets 10 RPS steady but spikes to 10,000 RPS during campaigns. What compute model do you choose?
**Answer:** This is a textbook serverless case. At 10 RPS steady, an always-on container would be 99% idle most of the time, paying for nothing. At 10,000 RPS spike, you need autoscaling that responds in seconds. Lambda fits both: it scales from a few concurrent invocations to thousands automatically, bills per request so steady-state cost is tiny, and zero when idle. The architecture: API Gateway (HTTP API for cost, REST API for features) → Lambda → DynamoDB (on-demand capacity) for state, with SQS as a buffer if downstream processing is slower than ingestion. Configure the Lambda with provisioned concurrency during known campaign windows to avoid cold starts, or rely on the burst allowance (3000 concurrent/sec) for unexpected spikes. Set up CloudWatch alarms on `Throttles` and `ConcurrentExecutions` to alert before hitting limits, and request a quota increase ahead of planned campaigns. The economic case is strong: 10 RPS steady is ~26M requests/month at 50ms each and 256MB, costing roughly $25/month — versus a multi-container always-on setup at $200+/month for the same peak capacity.
**Visual:**
```
campaign spike 10,000 RPS:
   API GW (HTTP) -> Lambda (burst to 3000 concurrent, scale to 10k)
                -> SQS (buffer) -> Lambda (drains at sustainable rate)
                -> DynamoDB on-demand (scales writes)
steady 10 RPS: ~$25/mo on Lambda vs $200+/mo on always-on containers
```

### Q7. Your Lambda writes to a relational database and you see connection exhaustion errors. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** Each Lambda execution environment opens its own database connection, and at high concurrency you can have hundreds or thousands of environments, each holding a connection — far exceeding the database's max connections. The fix is to centralize connection management. First, use Amazon RDS Proxy (or PgBouncer for non-RDS) which pools connections between Lambda and the database, multiplexing many Lambda connections onto a small pool of database connections. Second, ensure your Lambda code creates the database client at module scope (outside the handler) so each warm environment reuses one connection rather than opening a new one per invocation. Third, use Aurora Serverless v2 which scales both compute and connections. Fourth, consider whether a relational database is the right choice — DynamoDB handles connectionless access naturally and scales without connection limits. Fifth, if you must use a traditional RDS, scale up the instance to raise the max_connections setting, but this is treating the symptom. Netflix and Coca-Cola both route Lambda-to-RDS traffic through RDS Proxy or move state to DynamoDB to avoid this entirely.
**Visual:**
```
1000 Lambda envs x 1 conn each = 1000 conns -> RDS max=200 -> BOOM
fix:  RDS Proxy pools: 1000 Lambda conns -> ~50 DB conns
      + create DB client at module scope (reuse per warm env)
      + Aurora Serverless v2 (autoscaling connections)
      + DynamoDB (connectionless, scales without limit)
```
